title: The Black-Scholes Model
objectives: State the Black-Scholes assumptions and write down the pricing formula with d1 and d2
Interpret N(d1) as the call delta and N(d2) as the risk-neutral exercise probability
Compute a full option price by hand with every intermediate value carried explicitly
Verify the computed call and put against put-call parity
motivation: Every options screen in the world prints Black-Scholes numbers, more than fifty years after the paper. The model prices a European option as a discounted risk-neutral expectation under geometric Brownian motion, and the lognormal integral collapses into two normal CDF evaluations. We will compute one price completely by hand, every intermediate value shown to four decimals, so the formula stops being a black box, and then read N(d1) and N(d2) for what they really mean to a hedger.

blocks.md: Black-Scholes assumes the stock follows geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility $\sigma$, the risk-free rate $r$ is constant, there are no dividends or transaction costs, and trading is continuous. Under the risk-neutral measure, exactly the logic built node by node in the binomial lesson, the call's value is the discounted expected payoff $e^{-rT}\,E[\max(S_T - K, 0)]$. Because $S_T$ is lognormal, that expectation has a closed form, and the entire machinery of stochastic calculus condenses into five inputs and one formula.

blocks.tex: C = S_0\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rT}\,N(d_2), \qquad d_1 = \frac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)\,T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}
blocks.caption: $N(\cdot)$ is the standard normal CDF. The put follows by parity: $P = Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2) - S_0 N(-d_1)$.

blocks.md: Read the formula as a two-term ledger. $K e^{-rT} N(d_2)$ is the present value of the strike times the **risk-neutral probability of exercise** - $N(d_2)$ genuinely is $P^Q(S_T > K)$, because $d_2$ measures how many standard deviations the log-strike sits below the log-forward. $S_0 N(d_1)$ weights the stock by $N(d_1)$, which is the call's **delta**: the hedge ratio telling you how many shares replicate the option. The mysterious $\sigma^2/2$ inside $d_1$ is the lognormal convexity correction, it reflects that $E[S_T] = S_0 e^{rT}$ under $Q$, and the *log* of a lognormal has a $-\sigma^2/2$ drag. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not two probabilities of the same kind: one is a hedge ratio, one is an exercise probability.

blocks.title: S = 100, K = 100, r = 5% (continuous), sigma = 20%, T = 1 year
items: $\ln(S_0/K) = \ln(1) = 0$ - the option starts exactly at the money.
Parity check: $C - P = 10.45 - 5.57 = 4.88$ and $S - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 95.12 = 4.88$. Consistent, and at full machine precision the prices are 10.4506 and 5.5735.

blocks.caption: Reproduce the hand-computed 10.45, then push volatility from 20% to 30% and watch how much more the convexity of the payoff is suddenly worth.

blocks.title: Four inputs are observable; one is not
blocks.md: $S_0$, $K$, $T$ come from the contract, $r$ from the curve, but $\sigma$ is a guess. Turn the logic around: given a market price, solve for the volatility that reproduces it. That inversion is **implied volatility**, the subject of a later lesson, and it is the single most quoted number in derivatives markets.

blocks.title: Where hand computations go wrong
blocks.md: $N(d_1)$ is not the probability of exercise, that is $N(d_2)$ (for a European call, no dividends). Time must be in years with a consistent day count; volatility in the same annualized units. And if the stock pays dividends, subtract their present value from $S_0$ before applying the formula rather than pretending the input is clean.

blocks.code:
from math import log, sqrt, exp
from statistics import NormalDist

N = NormalDist().cdf

def bs_call(S, K, r, sigma, T):
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r + sigma * sigma / 2) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * sqrt(T)
    return S * N(d1) - K * exp(-r * T) * N(d2), d1, d2

price, d1, d2 = bs_call(100, 100, 0.05, 0.20, 1.0)
print(round(d1, 4))     # 0.35
print(round(d2, 4))     # 0.15
print(round(price, 4))  # 10.4506
blocks.caption: Twenty lines from the statistics standard library reproduce the benchmark price to four decimals.

blocks.md: The Black-Scholes formula is usually presented as an inscription to be admired. It is more useful as a *machine with four dials*, spot, strike, rate, volatility, time, where you can trace exactly which dial moves which output and why. The derivation belongs to a later lesson; here you learn to compute it, sanity-check it, and read the hedging information it carries, because that is what a desk actually uses it for.

blocks.title: Full computation: 1-year ATM call, S=K=100, r=5%, σ=20%
items: $d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T} = 0.350 - 0.200 = 0.150$. The gap between $d_1$ and $d_2$ is pure volatility-time, it is how much the distribution smears before expiry.

Same-parameters put: $P = \$5.57. Put-call parity check: $C - P = 4.88$ and $S - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 95.12 = 4.88$. Two completely different formulas agree to the cent, that is not luck, it is arbitrage enforcing internal consistency.

blocks.md: The two $N(\cdot)$ terms are not decoration. $N(d_1)$ is the **delta**: to hedge one short call you hold 0.637 shares, and that number *changes* as spot moves (that drift in delta is gamma, the hedging cost the formula anticipates). $N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money. When someone says "the market prices a 56% chance of expiring ITM", this is the sentence behind it.

blocks.title: Sanity checks you should run on any BSM number
blocks.md: Bounds: a European call must trade between $S - Ke^{-rT}$ and $S$, ours does ($4.88 \le 10.45 \le 100$). Monotonicity: raise σ and the call price must rise (volatility is the only dial that helps both calls and puts). ATM approximation: $C \approx 0.4 S\sigma\sqrt{T} = 0.4(100)(0.20)(1) = 8$, within 25% of our exact 10.45, which is close enough to catch order-of-magnitude errors instantly.

What the model *doesn't* claim is the part people misremember. It does not say prices are lognormal, it says **if** diffusion holds and hedging is continuous and costless, then this price is the replication cost. The formula is exact under its assumptions; the assumptions are the approximation. Every smile, skew and term structure you will meet later is the market's way of telling you where those assumptions leak.

guidedExercise.prompt: Reprice the same call ($S = 100$, $K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $T = 1$) with volatility raised to $\sigma = 30\%$. Compute $d_1$, $d_2$, the required $N$ values (given below) and the price.
guidedExercise.solution: $d_1 = (0.05 + 0.045)/(0.30 \times 1) = 0.095/0.30 = 0.3167$; $d_2 = 0.3167 - 0.30 = 0.0167$. $C = 100 \times 0.6243 - 100 \times 0.9512 \times 0.5067 = 62.43 - 48.20 = \$. The extra 10 volatility points added about \$3.78 of value, pure convexity, bought with time.

commonMistakes: Interpreting $N(d_1)$ as the probability of exercise, it is the delta; $N(d_2)$ is the exercise probability.
Mixing units: days for $T$ with annualized $\sigma$, or discrete compounding inside a continuous formula.
Dropping the $\sigma^2/2$ term from $d_1$ - at-the-money options are then mispriced by real money.
Forgetting that BS prices European options only: American features need trees or numerics.
realWorldApplication: Exchange-listed options are quoted in implied volatilities that are converted to prices with Black-Scholes (or close variants); even where models have moved on, BS remains the market's shared language for expressing and comparing option prices.
quantFinanceApplication: The derivation, risk-neutral expectation of a lognormal payoff, is the template for every closed-form model since: the same integration under a different $S_T$ distribution prices options under jumps, stochastic volatility and local vol.
summary: BS assumptions: GBM with constant $\sigma$ and $r$, no dividends, no frictions, European exercise.
$C = S_0 N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT} N(d_2)$ with $d_1 = [\ln(S/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, $d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}$.
$N(d_2)$ is the risk-neutral exercise probability; $N(d_1)$ is the call delta (hedge ratio); the $\sigma^2/2$ in $d_1$ is lognormal convexity.
Volatility is the only unobservable input, invert the model and you get implied volatility.

quiz.prompt: Using $K e^{-rT} = 95.12$, $N(-d_2) = 0.4404$, $N(-d_1) = 0.3632$ and $S = 100$: what is the European put price? (Two decimals.)
quiz.explanation: $P = 95.12 \times 0.4404 - 100 \times 0.3632 = 41.89 - 36.32 = 5.57$ - the put companion of the lesson's call.

quiz.prompt: In Black-Scholes, $N(d_2)$ for a European call (no dividends) represents:
options: The risk-neutral probability that the option finishes in the money
The stock's real-world probability of rising
quiz.explanation: $N(d_2) = P^Q(S_T > K)$, the probability-weighted discount factor on the strike. The delta is $N(d_1)$ - a related but distinct quantity.

quiz.prompt: As volatility approaches zero, a European call's Black-Scholes price approaches:
quiz.explanation: With no randomness the stock grows deterministically to $S_0 e^{rT}$; the call is worth the discounted positive part of the forward minus strike. Uncertainty, not the direction of the stock, is what the time value prices.

quiz.prompt: Which inputs does the Black-Scholes formula require?
quiz.explanation: $S_0$, $\sigma$, $r$ (plus contract-defined $K$, $T$). The expected return famously does not appear: hedging removes the drift's influence on value.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why the stock's expected return does not appear anywhere in the Black-Scholes formula.
quiz.modelAnswer: Continuous delta-hedging replicates the option's payoffs with stock and bonds, so its value is pinned by arbitrage alone; expectations only enter through the risk-neutral measure where all assets earn r, replacing the real-world drift.
quiz.explanation: The same logic as the binomial tree, taken to continuous time: replication kills the dependence on real-world probabilities, leaving only $r$, $\sigma$ and the contract terms.

flashcards.back: $N(d_2)$ = risk-neutral probability of exercise (European call, no dividends); $N(d_1)$ = call delta / hedge ratio.
$P = Ke^{-rT} N(-d_2) - S_0 N(-d_1)$; always check $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$.
Lognormal convexity: $E[S_T] = S_0 e^{rT}$ under Q, so the log-forward is shifted down by $\sigma^2/2 T$; d1 measures distance to the strike in standard deviations of the log.

references.label: Black & Scholes (1973): The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities
